chunks: "A trigger tells the scope when to start drawing. Without it, each sweep starts at a random point in the waveform, so a repeating signal smears or scrolls.
With an edge trigger, I choose the source channel, a voltage level and a slope, rising or falling, and the scope starts every sweep exactly when the signal crosses that level in that direction.
Every sweep lines up, so the waveform looks stationary.
To use it, I pick the channel I care about, set the level somewhere in the middle of the edge, well clear of noise, and choose the slope.
For a normal repeating signal I use auto or normal mode; if the event only happens once, I use single mode, which arms, waits, captures one record and stops.
If a signal has bursts, I add holdoff so it triggers on the first pulse of a burst only.

Beyond edge triggers, I'd use pulse-width or runt triggers to catch bad pulses, a timeout trigger to find a signal that stopped toggling, and serial triggers to catch a specific I²C address or an error.
And because the scope keeps pre-trigger data, I can trigger on the symptom, like a reset line falling, and look backwards at what the supply was doing."
